title: Carbohydrates: One Bond Decides Fuel or Fiber

generated.pipeline: extract → Opus draft → Sonnet accuracy gate → Sonnet fixes

cards.front: Classify glucose and fructose by carbonyl type and carbon count. What isomer relationship do they share?
cards.back: Glucose is an aldohexose (aldehyde at C1); fructose is a ketohexose (ketone at C2). Same formula, carbonyl on a different carbon: constitutional isomers.
cards.quote: Glucose and fructose have the same formula but the carbonyl on a different carbon, which makes them constitutional isomers.
cards.section: Meet glucose: just enough to number it

cards.front: Whether a sugar is D or L is set by the chiral carbon {{c1::farthest from the carbonyl}}.
cards.back: Biology runs almost entirely on D-sugars.
cards.quote: Whether a sugar is D or L is set by the chiral carbon farthest from the carbonyl
cards.section: Meet glucose: just enough to number it

cards.front: In water, how does linear glucose close into a ring, and what kind of group does that form? What forms for a ketose such as fructose?
cards.back: The C5 hydroxyl attacks the C1 aldehyde, spontaneously and with no enzyme, giving a six-membered ring. Alcohol plus aldehyde makes a hemiacetal; a ketose makes a hemiketal.
cards.quote: An alcohol adding to an aldehyde makes a hemiacetal.
cards.section: Closing the ring makes one special carbon

cards.front: What is the anomeric carbon of a cyclic sugar, and which carbon is it in glucose and in fructose?
cards.back: The old carbonyl carbon, which becomes a new chiral center when the ring closes. C1 in glucose, C2 in fructose.
cards.quote: the old carbonyl carbon now carries four different groups and becomes a new chiral center, the anomeric carbon
cards.section: Closing the ring makes one special carbon

cards.front: In a cyclic D-sugar, how are the α and β anomers defined?
cards.back: α: the C1 hydroxyl is on the opposite face of the ring from the CH₂OH (C6) on C5. β: it is on the same face.
cards.quote: α: the C1 hydroxyl is on the opposite face of the ring from the CH₂OH group (C6) on C5.
cards.section: Closing the ring makes one special carbon

cards.front: A Haworth drawing of D-glucopyranose is printed upside down, so the CH₂OH on C5 points down and the C1 hydroxyl points up, on the opposite face. Which anomer is it?
cards.back: α. The anomer is set by the C1 hydroxyl's face relative to the CH₂OH, not by up or down on the page; opposite faces means α.
cards.quote: Flip the drawing and "below" flips too; the CH₂OH reference does not.
cards.section: Closing the ring makes one special carbon

cards.front: A glucose solution at equilibrium is about 36:64 α:β, with well under 1% open chain. Why does β predominate?
cards.back: Mostly because, in the chair, β-glucose puts every bulky group, including the C1 hydroxyl, equatorial, where groups crowd each other least (the anomeric effect keeps the preference modest). In α-glucose the C1 hydroxyl is axial.
cards.quote: β wins mostly because every bulky group, the C1 hydroxyl included, sits equatorial.
cards.section: Closing the ring makes one special carbon

cards.front: Glucose anomers settle at 36:64 α:β at 25 °C. Estimate the standard free-energy difference favoring β (R = 8.314 J/mol·K).
cards.back: K = 64/36 ≈ 1.78. ΔG° = −RT ln K = −(8.314)(298 K)(ln 1.78) ≈ −1.4 kJ/mol, a small preference for β.
cards.quote: The 36:64 α:β ratio is a small energy difference, about 1.4 kJ/mol in favor of β at 25 °C.
cards.section: Why the split is not more lopsided

cards.front: What are epimers? Name glucose's C2 epimer and its C4 epimer.
cards.back: Stereoisomers that differ at exactly one chiral center. Mannose is glucose's C2 epimer; galactose is its C4 epimer.
cards.quote: Glucose and mannose (C2); glucose and galactose (C4)
cards.section: Naming the relationships

cards.front: Glucose differs from mannose at C2 and from galactose at C4. What is the relationship between mannose and galactose?
cards.back: Diastereomers but not epimers: they differ at two chiral centers (C2 and C4) and are not mirror images.
cards.why: Epimers differ at exactly one chiral center; enantiomers differ at every one.
cards.quote: Stereoisomers that are not mirror images (the umbrella for the next two rows)
cards.section: Naming the relationships

cards.front: Pure α-glucose crystals are dissolved in water. What is the mixture the next day, and what is the process called?
cards.back: About one-third α, two-thirds β and a trace of open chain. The ring keeps reopening and can reclose on either face: mutarotation.
cards.quote: This drift is called mutarotation, after the change in how the solution rotates polarized light.
cards.section: A free anomeric carbon can reopen

cards.front: Glucose is under 1% open chain at any instant. Why is it still a reducing sugar?
cards.back: Because it can become open chain. The free anomeric carbon lets the ring reopen, exposing an aldehyde that gives up electrons.
cards.quote: Glucose is reducing not because it is usually open-chain, but because it can become open-chain.
cards.section: A free anomeric carbon can reopen

cards.front: In Benedict's test, what color change marks a reducing sugar, and what is reduced?
cards.back: Blue to brick-red. Blue Cu(II) takes electrons from the sugar's aldehyde and becomes brick-red Cu₂O; the aldehyde is oxidized.
cards.quote: In Benedict's test, blue Cu(II) takes those electrons and becomes brick-red Cu₂O.
cards.section: A free anomeric carbon can reopen

cards.front: What is HbA1c chemically, and why does it report average blood glucose over the prior two to three months?
cards.back: Glucose attached non-enzymatically to the N-terminal valine of hemoglobin's β chain. Red cells live about 120 days, so the tag accumulates over that window.
cards.quote: Red cells live about 120 days, so HbA1c is a molecular diary of your average blood glucose over the prior two to three months
cards.section: The clinic hiding in "under one percent"

cards.front: A protein is incubated for weeks with either glucose or sucrose at equal concentration. Which sugar glycates its free amino groups directly, and why?
cards.back: Glucose. Glycation runs through the open-chain aldehyde; glucose's free anomeric carbon lets its ring open, while both anomeric carbons of sucrose are locked in its glycosidic bond.
cards.why: Rests on two rules: protein glycation uses the open-chain aldehyde, and a used anomeric carbon cannot reopen.
cards.quote: The open-chain aldehyde reacts slowly and non-enzymatically with free amino groups on proteins.
cards.section: The clinic hiding in "under one percent"

cards.front: A patient's red cells survive only about 60 days. How would HbA1c misreport average blood glucose, and why?
cards.back: It would likely read lower than the true average. Glycation accumulates over a red cell's life, and cells that live shorter have less time to collect glucose.
cards.why: Rests on HbA1c as a small open-chain fraction multiplied by months of exposure over a roughly 120-day cell life.
cards.quote: A vanishingly small open-chain fraction, multiplied by months of exposure, becomes a clinical number.
cards.section: The clinic hiding in "under one percent"

cards.front: In the glycosidic linkage name α-1,4, what do the 1, the α and the 4 each mean?
cards.back: 1: the anomeric carbon (C1) of the first sugar. α: the face that bond leaves from. 4: the carbon it joins on the next sugar (C4).
cards.quote: the Greek letter is the face that bond leaves from, and the second number is the carbon it joins on the next sugar (C4)
cards.section: A used anomeric carbon: the glycosidic bond

cards.front: What structural rule decides whether a disaccharide is a reducing sugar?
cards.back: It is reducing if at least one anomeric carbon is still free to open. A used anomeric carbon is locked in the glycosidic bond and cannot open.
cards.quote: a sugar is reducing if at least one anomeric carbon is still free to open.
cards.section: A used anomeric carbon: the glycosidic bond

cards.front: Why does sucrose (glucose α-1,β-2 fructose) leave Benedict's reagent blue while maltose (glucose α-1,4 glucose) turns it brick-red?
cards.back: Sucrose's bond joins both anomeric carbons, C1 of glucose and C2 of fructose, so neither ring can open. Maltose's receiving glucose keeps a free anomeric carbon.
cards.quote: Here both numbers are anomeric carbons: C1 of glucose and C2 of fructose, the ketose.
cards.section: A used anomeric carbon: the glycosidic bond

cards.front: A hypothetical disaccharide joins two glucoses from C1 of one to C1 of the other. Would it give a positive Benedict's test?
cards.back: No. Both anomeric carbons are used in the glycosidic bond, so neither ring can open to an aldehyde.
cards.why: A sugar is reducing only if at least one anomeric carbon is free.
cards.quote: Once the anomeric carbon is used this way, its ring can no longer open.
cards.section: A used anomeric carbon: the glycosidic bond

cards.front: What are lactose's two sugars and linkage, and which enzyme cleaves it, where?
cards.back: Galactose-glucose, β-1,4. Lactase on the small-intestine brush border cleaves it; losing lactase in adulthood can cause lactose intolerance.
cards.quote: Lactase, an enzyme on the lining of the small intestine (the brush border), cleaves it.
cards.section: A used anomeric carbon: the glycosidic bond

cards.front: A hypothetical disaccharide is glucose joined β-1,4 to glucose. Is it a reducing sugar, and would human amylase cleave it?
cards.back: Reducing, but not cleaved by amylase. The receiving glucose keeps a free anomeric carbon; amylases fit α-1,4 geometry, and β-1,4 is the cellulose bond.
cards.why: Two rules: one free anomeric carbon makes a sugar reducing; an enzyme's active site fits one bond geometry.
cards.quote: Your amylases fit α-1,4, and they cut it in the middle of chains, not end by end.
cards.section: Bond geometry sets polymer shape

cards.front: Why does a β-1,4 glucose chain run straight while an α-1,4 chain coils into a helix?
cards.back: In β-glucose the C1 and C4 bonds are both equatorial and point in opposite directions, so the chain passes straight through. In α-glucose the C1 bond is axial, so every junction bends the same way.
cards.quote: In β-glucose the bond leaving C1 is equatorial, and so is the bond at C4.
cards.section: Bond geometry sets polymer shape

cards.front: How does chain shape make cellulose structural but starch and glycogen storage forms?
cards.back: Flat β-1,4 ribbons lie side by side and hydrogen-bond into rigid fibrils. An α-1,4 helix cannot lie flat that way, so it packs into compact granules or particles.
cards.quote: Flat β-1,4 ribbons lie side by side and hydrogen-bond into rigid fibrils.
cards.section: Bond geometry sets polymer shape

cards.front: Starch and cellulose are both pure glucose. Why can humans digest starch but not cellulose?
cards.back: Digestion needs an enzyme whose active site fits the bond. Our amylases fit α-1,4; we make no cellulase for β-1,4. Packed cellulose fibrils also break down slowly.
cards.why: A cow digests grass because rumen microbes make cellulases for it.
cards.quote: You make no cellulase, the enzyme that cuts the β-1,4 bonds between the glucoses of cellulose.
cards.section: Bond geometry sets polymer shape

cards.front: Suppose an active cellulase were supplied in the human gut. Predict how readily glucose would be released from dietary cellulose.
cards.back: Probably slowly. The enzyme could cut β-1,4 bonds, yet tightly bonded cellulose fibrils resist breakdown even for microbes that have the enzyme.
cards.quote: Packing adds to the problem: tightly bonded cellulose fibrils break down slowly even for microbes that have the enzyme.
cards.section: Bond geometry sets polymer shape

cards.front: A student claims every β-linked glucose polymer forms straight, flat fibrils like cellulose. Is that right?
cards.back: No. The straight-versus-helix result holds for 1,4-linked glucose. β-1,3 glucans, such as callose in plants and bacterial curdlan, form helices.
cards.quote: This straight-versus-helix result is for 1,4-linked glucose, not a general law
cards.section: Bond geometry sets polymer shape

cards.front: Which linkage makes the branch points of glycogen and amylopectin, and how often does each branch? Does amylose branch?
cards.back: α-1,6. Glycogen every 8 to 12 residues (about ten), amylopectin about every thirty. Amylose stays linear.
cards.quote: Glycogen branches every 8 to 12 residues (often rounded to about ten), amylopectin about every thirty, and amylose stays linear.
cards.section: Branching: more ends, faster fuel

cards.front: A glycogen particle has 99 α-1,6 branch points. How many non-reducing ends and reducing ends does it have?
cards.back: Non-reducing ends = b + 1 = 99 + 1 = 100. Reducing ends = 1, however many branches.
cards.why: Each branch point uses one more anomeric carbon and starts one more chain.
cards.quote: A glucan with b branch points has b + 1 non-reducing ends and one reducing end.
cards.section: Branching: more ends, faster fuel

cards.front: Why does a branched glycogen particle release glucose faster than an unbranched chain of the same size?
cards.back: Glycogen phosphorylase works only from non-reducing ends. The chain has one; the particle has b + 1, so many enzyme molecules work at once.
cards.quote: The single chain offers one non-reducing end; the particle offers b + 1, so many enzyme molecules work at once.
cards.section: Branching: more ends, faster fuel

cards.front: In glycogen breakdown, where does phosphorylase stop, and what removes the α-1,6 branch bonds?
cards.back: Phosphorylase stops a few residues short of each branch; a separate debranching enzyme handles the α-1,6 bond.
cards.quote: It stops a few residues short of each branch, and a separate debranching enzyme handles the α-1,6 bond.
cards.section: Branching: more ends, faster fuel

cards.front: A cell has normal glycogen synthase but no branching enzyme. Predict its glycogen's structure and how fast it can be mobilized.
cards.back: Long, unbranched α-1,4 chains with few non-reducing ends, so few phosphorylase molecules can work at once and glucose release is slow.
cards.why: Glycogen synthase adds glucose (from UDP-glucose) to non-reducing ends; only the branching enzyme installs α-1,6 links.
cards.quote: a separate branching enzyme installs the α-1,6 links
cards.section: Branching: more ends, faster fuel

cards.front: Muscle lacks debranching enzyme but has normal phosphorylase. Predict glucose release from glycogen during a sprint.
cards.back: Glucose release stalls: phosphorylase stops a few residues short of each branch, and nothing cleaves the α-1,6 bonds, so the inner glycogen stays locked.
cards.why: Rests on phosphorylase working only from non-reducing ends and a separate debranching enzyme handling α-1,6 bonds.
cards.quote: The enzyme that releases glucose, glycogen phosphorylase, works only from non-reducing ends.
cards.section: Branching: more ends, faster fuel

cards.front: Imagine an enzyme that released glucose only from reducing ends. Would branching a glycogen particle speed its work?
cards.back: No. Branching adds non-reducing ends (b + 1), but a whole branched particle still has just one reducing end, so the enzyme would have a single site.
cards.quote: A whole branched particle has just one.
cards.section: Branching: more ends, faster fuel

cards.front: A glycogen model has 12 tiers of 13-residue chains, each inner chain carrying two branches. How many chains, glucoses, outer chains and branch points?
cards.back: Chains = 2¹² − 1 = 4,095. Glucoses = 4,095 × 13 = 53,235. Outer chains = 2¹¹ = 2,048. Branch points = chains − 1 = 4,094.
cards.quote: Build 12 tiers of 13-residue chains, each inner chain carrying two branches: that gives 4,095 chains, 53,235 glucoses and 2,048 outer chains.
cards.section: Glycogen particle size: a model

cards.front: Fat packs more energy per gram. Why does a sprint draw on glycogen rather than fat?
cards.back: Glucose mobilizes faster. A sprint uses phosphocreatine and glycogen through glycolysis; fat oxidation is too slow and needs oxygen.
cards.quote: fat oxidation is too slow and needs oxygen
cards.section: Sugar or fat for a sprint

cards.front: To which amino acid do N-linked glycans attach, and within what consensus sequence?
cards.back: Asparagine, almost always in asparagine, then any residue except proline, then serine or threonine.
cards.quote: N-linked glycans attach to asparagine, almost always within a consensus sequence
cards.section: The sugar coat: a second rule

cards.front: A glycoprotein carries the sequence Asn-Pro-Ser. Is that asparagine likely to be N-glycosylated?
cards.back: No. The middle position may be any residue except proline, so Asn-Pro-Ser breaks the consensus.
cards.quote: asparagine, then any residue except proline, then serine or threonine
cards.section: The sugar coat: a second rule

cards.front: To which amino acids do O-linked glycans attach, and do they need a consensus sequence?
cards.back: Serine or threonine. They follow no single consensus sequence.
cards.quote: O-linked glycans attach to serine or threonine and follow no single consensus sequence.
cards.section: The sugar coat: a second rule

cards.front: In the ABO system, what sugar does each allele's glycosyltransferase add to the H antigen?
cards.back: A adds N-acetylgalactosamine; B adds galactose; O adds nothing. A and B use the same α1-3 bond.
cards.quote: The A enzyme adds N-acetylgalactosamine, the B enzyme adds galactose, and the O allele adds nothing.
cards.section: The sugar coat: a second rule

cards.front: A person inherits two O alleles. What sits at the tip of the ABO antigen on their red cells?
cards.back: The unmodified H antigen. The O allele adds nothing, so neither N-acetylgalactosamine (A) nor galactose (B) is attached.
cards.quote: acting on a shared core antigen called the H antigen
cards.section: The sugar coat: a second rule

cards.front: A cell cannot add mannose-6-phosphate tags to its newly made lysosomal enzymes. Where do those enzymes end up?
cards.back: Outside the cell, in the blood, instead of in lysosomes. Mannose-6-phosphate is their lysosome address; losing it causes I-cell disease.
cards.quote: A mannose-6-phosphate tag is the address that routes enzymes to the lysosome.
cards.section: The sugar coat: a second rule

cards.front: A single sugar-protein grip is weak, typically with Kd in the micromolar to millimolar range. How do lectins bind cell surfaces strongly and selectively?
cards.back: Multivalency: many weak handholds at once add up to a strong, selective grip, like hook-and-loop fastener.
cards.quote: Lectins solve that with multivalency: many weak handholds at once add up to a strong, selective grip
cards.section: Lectins read what the sugar code wrote

cards.front: A lectin is engineered to keep only one of its sugar-binding sites. Predict how well it binds a cell's sugar coat.
cards.back: Weakly. A single sugar-protein grip typically has a Kd in the micromolar to millimolar range; without many simultaneous handholds the strong, selective grip is lost.
cards.quote: Any one sugar-protein grip is weak, typically with a dissociation constant (Kd) in the micromolar to millimolar range.
cards.section: Lectins read what the sugar code wrote

cards.front: In influenza infection, what do hemagglutinin and neuraminidase each do, and which does oseltamivir block?
cards.back: Hemagglutinin, a lectin, binds sialic acid to latch onto airway cells. Neuraminidase cuts new virions free to leave. Oseltamivir inhibits neuraminidase, slowing release and spread.
cards.quote: To leave, new virions must cut themselves free, which is the job of the viral enzyme neuraminidase.
cards.section: Lectins read what the sugar code wrote

cards.front: A lectin's grip on a single sugar is weak. Why can it still bind a cell surface strongly?
cards.back: Multivalency: many weak handholds at once add up to a strong, selective grip. Each single sugar-lectin grip is weak (Kd typically micromolar to millimolar).
cards.why: Rests on the multivalency rule for lectins.
cards.quote: Lectins solve that with multivalency: many weak handholds at once add up to a strong, selective grip
cards.section: Lectins read what the sugar code wrote
